records.why: The text said the leaf rises further when a negative strip is brought near an electroscope that is positive, and used that to 'show' it is positive. That is wrong and contradicts Lesson 8 and the sentence in brackets. On a positive electroscope (deficit of electrons) a negative object pushes electrons down to the leaf, cancelling its positive charge, so the leaf falls; a positive object pulls electrons up to the cap and the leaf rises. Checked twice by tracing electron movement for both objects, and against Lesson 8 (rise = same sign, fall = opposite sign).
records.old: Sign test: bring the negative strip near again, and the leaf rises further (above 30 degrees), which shows the electroscope is now positively charged. (Learners are told that the leaf rises above 30 degrees when a negative object is brought near an electroscope that is already negative; for a positive electroscope the effect is the opposite, so they compare this with the earlier data and discuss in the Explain phase.)
records.new: Sign test (the electroscope is now positive, at about 30 degrees): bring the negative strip near the cap again and the leaf falls below 30 degrees; then bring a rubbed perspex rod (positive, rubbed with silk) near the cap and the leaf rises above 30 degrees. A fall with a negative object and a rise with a positive object shows that the electroscope is positively charged, the opposite sign to the strip. Learners compare this with the earlier data and discuss why in the Explain phase; the sign test is developed fully in Lesson 8.
records.reference: OpenStax College Physics, Chapter 18 'Electric Charge and Electric Field', sections 18.1-18.2 (charging by induction and the electroscope)

records.why: The rubric used the labels excellent / proficient / developing. The contract keeps those three fields, so each descriptor now starts with the CBE level name; the criteria text itself is unchanged.

value.criterion: Origin of charge (electron transfer and conservation)
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly explains that charges come from electrons already in atoms, that electrons move from hair to latex and protons stay put, uses the triboelectric order and the 1 nC, 6 x 10^9 electrons, 10^23 atoms figures, and states that charge is transferred, not created.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains that electrons transfer from hair to balloon so the balloon is negative and hair positive, and mentions that charge is conserved, but gives few or no numbers or no reason from the triboelectric order.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Says that rubbing creates charge or does not say what moves, or mixes up which object is positive and which is negative. If none of this is shown, the work is at the Below Expectations level.

value.criterion: Attraction and repulsion, including neutral objects
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses like-repel and unlike-attract with evidence from the rods and strips, and explains attraction of neutral paper and wall by induction (charge separation, nearer charge attracts more), with a labelled particle diagram and the point that neutral objects are never repelled.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Applies the rule to balloons and hair and mentions that neutral objects are attracted because of charge separation, but with limited detail or no diagram.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Only describes attraction and repulsion without giving a cause, or says that neutral objects are repelled or that positive charge moves. If none of this is shown, the work is at the Below Expectations level.

value.criterion: Conductors, insulators, charging methods and distribution
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly links free versus tightly bound electrons to the conduction test and to the balloon keeping its charge, and compares contact (same sign) with induction and earthing (opposite sign). Explains charge on outer surfaces and at points with point discharge, using the electroscope and proof-plane readings.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Correctly states the difference between conductors and insulators and between contact and induction, and gives some of the readings, with some gaps in explaining distribution or earthing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses conductors with insulators or contact with induction, or gives no use of the readings. If none of this is shown, the work is at the Below Expectations level.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains the electroscope (same sign on leaf and stem, bigger angle means more charge, sign test, earthing), explains humidity using 35% and 80% and the 3 minutes against under 30 seconds figures, and links two applications to the correct idea.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains how the electroscope detects charge and mentions humidity and one application correctly, with few data values.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Does not explain how the electroscope works or the effect of humidity, or applications are not linked to electrostatics ideas. If none of this is shown, the work is at the Below Expectations level.

value.criterion: Use of evidence, vocabulary and coherence
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses exact data and lesson evidence, uses terms such as electric charge, electrostatic force, discharge, earthing and induction accurately, and gives a connected final answer that shows how the Lesson 1 model has changed.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses most evidence and terms correctly and gives a mostly connected answer.

records.why: Journal item phys_3_4-048 (teacher: Physics). KICD lists charging a conductor by contact, induction AND separation; separation was untaught. Added as a short teacher demonstration (standard two-conductor separation: near conductor ends with a deficit, far one with the excess, equal and opposite; checked by conservation of charge). Teacher decides whether cans, insulating supports and an electroscope are available; if not, diagram only.
records.old: Check that learners are only touching the cap when instructed.
records.new: Check that learners are only touching the cap when instructed. Separation demonstration (about 4 minutes, in the sharing time, by the teacher): stand two clean, dry metal cans touching, each on a dry plastic cup or block. Bring a rubbed negative polythene strip near the first can without touching. With the strip still near, pull the cans apart using the insulating supports, then remove the strip. Touch each can to the cap of a fresh neutral electroscope: the leaf rises both times, so both cans are charged. Learners cannot tell the signs from the leaf yet (the sign test is Lesson 8), so the signs come from the diagram: electrons were pushed from the near can to the far can, so the near can has a deficit (positive) and the far can an excess (negative), equal in size. If it will not fit or the cans are damp, show it as a diagram only in Explain Task 3.
records.group_headline: Added charging by separation (KICD names it with contact and induction) to Lesson 6 as a short teacher demonstration and a three-way comparison
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 curriculum design, Physics, Strand 3.0 Electricity and Magnetism, Sub-strand 3.1 Electrostatics; OpenStax College Physics, Chapter 18 Electric Charge and Electric Field

records.why: Journal item phys_3_4-048 (teacher: Physics). KICD lists Electric field patterns but no lesson taught them, and Lesson 7 already used the phrase strong field at a point. Added a 5-minute field-line sketch. Convention checked: field lines show force on a positive test charge, start on positive and end on negative, never cross, closer = stronger.
records.old: with lightning a much larger one.
records.new: with lightning a much larger one. Field patterns (about 5 minutes, from a teacher drawing or a simulation if one is available; time comes from the discussion in this phase): learners sketch electric field lines around a single positive charge, a single negative charge, a positive and a negative charge side by side, and two like charges. They note: the lines show the direction of the force on a small positive test charge, so they point away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge; between unlike charges they curve from the positive to the negative; between like charges they bend away from each other; lines never cross; where the lines are closer together the force is stronger. They link this to the pear-shaped conductor: the lines crowd at the point, where the field is strongest.
